subject: mathematics
question_text: If A, B, C are angles in a triangle, prove that sin A + sin B − sin C = 4 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) cos(C/2).

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.108 — from the book's separate "STAR QUESTIONS PLUS" bank, answer 171. That bank (book pp.98-111, answers 142-180) sits AFTER all the numbered chapters and is organised by chapter rather than forming part of any chapter's own inventory; it is authored into this unit because that is where the question belongs on the paper (founder decision 2026-08-22). SECTION: classed LAQ on its length and shape — a transformation identity on a triangle, the exact shape of Unit 6's own LAQ chapter. The bank prints no mark cut, so this classification is OURS. Printed appearances: none — this answer carries no year tag. The MINUS in front of sin C is what puts sines rather than cosines on the right-hand side. The same question with a plus would end in cosines. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — the bank prints no [N Marks] tags anywhere. The shapes used follow the splits the book DOES print elsewhere: 1+1 for a 2-mark VSAQ (answers 100, 101 on book p.82), 1+1+1+1 or 1+2+1 for a 4-mark SAQ (answers 58, 59 on p.63 and 61 on p.64), and the granular split for a 7-mark LAQ (answer 32 on p.44). This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Replace sin(C/2) inside.

recall_prompt: Say how you would do this one — name each move in order.

steps.label: Group the first two terms
steps.margin_note: Two of the eight marks. sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A+B)/2) cos((A−B)/2), with sin C left outside for now.
lines: L.H.S = (sin A + sin B) − sin C

recall.must_convey: That sin A + sin B becomes 2 sin((A+B)/2) cos((A−B)/2).
accept: group the first two and apply sin plus sin to get two sin of A plus B by two into cos of A minus B by two
apply the sum to product formula to the first pair
leave sin C outside for now
modati rendu group chesi sum to product apply cheyyali
convert the first pair to a product
heard_as: two sin A plus B by two
cos A minus B by two

steps.why: Halving the angle sum gives 90°, which is the fact every later substitution leans on. Writing it at the start saves repeating it.

steps.label: Replace (A+B)/2 by 90° − C/2
steps.margin_note: Third mark. (A+B)/2 = 90° − C/2, and sin(90° − θ) = cos θ.

accept: A plus B by two is ninety minus C by two so its sine is cos C by two
sin of ninety minus theta is cos theta
use the half angle sum to turn the sine into a cosine
A plus B by two ante ninety minus C by two, sin adi cos C by two
apply the half angle sum

steps.why: The right-hand side ends in cos(C/2), and this is where that factor first appears. Everything after this keeps it.

steps.label: Expand sin C and factor
steps.margin_note: Two marks. sin C = 2 sin(C/2) cos(C/2), so both terms carry 2 cos(C/2) — take it out.

recall.must_convey: That sin C = 2 sin(C/2) cos(C/2), and 2 cos(C/2) is factored out.
accept: sin C is two sin C by two cos C by two so both terms have two cos C by two which comes out
expand sin C as a double angle then factor
the bracket is cos of A minus B by two minus sin C by two
sin C ni double angle ga rasi two cos C by two common teeyali
expand and factor

steps.why: sin C has to be written in HALF angles before anything can be factored — the rest of the expression is already in halves and C is not.
common_mistakes: Writing sin C = sin(C/2) cos(C/2) without the 2.

steps.label: Replace sin(C/2) inside
steps.margin_note: Two marks (sixth and seventh). Inside the bracket, sin(C/2) = sin(90° − (A+B)/2) = cos((A+B)/2) — so both terms are cosines.

recall.must_convey: That sin(C/2) inside the bracket becomes cos((A+B)/2), giving a difference of two cosines.
accept: sin C by two inside the bracket becomes cos of A plus B by two
reverse the substitution inside the bracket only
the bracket becomes a difference of two cosines
bracket lo sin C by two ni cos A plus B by two ga marchali
substitute inside the bracket
heard_as: cos A plus B by two

steps.why: The cos(C/2) outside is kept and the sin(C/2) inside is converted. The same angle is treated two ways because the bracket needs matching functions.
common_mistakes: Converting the cos(C/2) outside as well.

steps.label: Apply the difference formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. cos X − cos Y with X = (A−B)/2, Y = (A+B)/2 gives 2 sin(A/2) sin(B/2).

lines.text: ∴ sin A + sin B − sin C = 4 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) cos(C/2)

recall.must_convey: That the bracket is 2 sin(A/2) sin(B/2), giving 4 sin(A/2) sin(B/2) cos(C/2).
accept: the bracket is two sin A by two sin B by two so the answer is four sin A by two sin B by two cos C by two
a difference of cosines gives a product of sines
the two twos multiply to four
bracket two sin A by two sin B by two, rendu twos four
close the proof

steps.why: A DIFFERENCE of cosines gives sines; a SUM gives cosines. That is why the minus in the question puts sines on the right-hand side.
common_mistakes: Getting the bracket order backwards and losing a sign.
